neutral_facts.value: The accused was prosecuted for rape. The prosecution alleged that the accused committed rape on the prosecutrix. The prosecutrix immediately after returning home narrated the incident to her mother-in-law. One day after the incident, when her husband returned home, she lodged an FIR. The medical report did not give a definite opinion on whether she suffered sexual intercourse, but the FSL report confirmed spots of semen and spermatozoa on her petticoat. The trial court acquitted the accused on the ground that sexual intercourse was with the consent of the prosecutrix. The High Court convicted the accused. The prosecutrix stated that the accused fell her down, covered her mouth, restricted her hands, and committed rape. The FIR and evidence of the prosecutrix's mother-in-law corroborated her statement. The FSL report confirmed sexual intercourse. The accused did not present a defense of consent and claimed he was falsely implicated due to a quarrel with the prosecutrix's husband, but this defense was not supported by evidence.

key_evidence_accepted.value: The prosecutrix's evidence is reliable and corroborated by the evidence of PW2, the FIR, and the FSL report. The forensic evidence confirms spots of semen and spermatozoa on the petticoat of the prosecutrix.

quotes.text: The evidence of PW-5, in the present case, is also corroborated by other evidence. Section 157 of the Evidence Act provides that in order to corroborate the testimony of a witness, any former statement made by such witness relating to the same fact at or about the time when the fact took place, or before any authority legally competent to investigate the fact may be proved.

witness_credibility.value: The prosecutrix is a competent witness under Section 118 of the Evidence Act and her evidence must receive the same weight as that of an injured witness. Her testimony is corroborated by PW2 and the FIR.

quotes.text: The prosecutrix is a victim of, and not an accomplice in, a sex offence and there is no provision in the Evidence Act requiring corroboration in material particulars of the evidence of the prosecutrix as is in the case of evidence of accomplice. The prosecutrix is thus a competent witness under Section 118 of the Evidence Act and her evidence must receive the same weight as is attached to an injured witness in cases of physical violence.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the accused committed rape on PW5-prosecutrix, and the evidence of PW5 is reliable and corroborated by PW2, the FIR, and the FSL report. The prosecution case was proved beyond reasonable doubt.

quotes.text: The evidence of the prosecutrix is reliable - The same is corroborated by evidence of PW2, the FIR and the FSL report - Prosecution case is proved beyond reasonable doubt - Accused is liable to be convicted.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the trial court was correct in acquitting the accused as there was no proof of rape, the medical examination did not show injuries, and the prosecutrix omitted to mention the seizure of items in her evidence. The investigation was deemed defective and cast doubt on the prosecution case.

quotes.text: The trial court was not correct in recording the finding that there was consent of PW-5 to the sexual intercourse committed by the appellant.

legal_principle_applied.value: The court applied the principle that the prosecutrix is a victim and not an accomplice, and her evidence does not require corroboration as it does in the case of an accomplice. The court also emphasized that the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

quotes.text: The prosecutrix is a victim of, and not an accomplice in, a sex offence and there is no provision in the Evidence Act requiring corroboration in material particulars of the evidence of the prosecutrix as is in the case of evidence of accomplice.
